title: Spain’s inflation shock hit the shopping basket and the balance sheet
summary: A VAT cut makes essential purchases cheaper. A targeted transfer leaves the posted price in place and puts income in the hands of eligible households. In a Banco de España working paper, Myroslav Pidkuyko and Raffaele Rossi ask which instrument would have provided better household insurance during Spain’s 2021–23 cost-of-living shock if each had the same fiscal cost in every period. Their central estimate is that a transfer expansion would have delivered about twice the improvement in aggregate welfare. The result belongs to the authors’ Spanish household model. Households value the instrument through its effects on their consumption, saving and work decisions over time.

The exercise begins with households distributed by age, earnings, assets, family size and education. Spanish household surveys supply information about spending baskets and income. Food and energy take up larger shares of a constrained household’s budget. Each household can change what it buys, how much it saves and, where the model permits, whether to work. The inflation shock is initially unexpected. After its arrival households know the remaining aggregate path in the simulation. Spain takes the nominal interest rate as given within the monetary union. This isolates how an imported price shock redistributes welfare through household finances. It leaves the ECB’s response and any effect of national transfers on the aggregate price level outside the exercise.

Without the discretionary policies, the authors obtain a 6.65% consumption-equivalent loss. This expresses the loss in welfare as a uniform adjustment to consumption. It is not the cumulative inflation rate or a measured 6.65% decline in spending. Table 4 decomposes this loss. Differential inflation across goods contributes about 0.30 percentage points, erosion of real income 1.94 points, changes in the real value of nominal assets and debts 2.02 points, and tax and benefit thresholds failing to keep pace with inflation 2.39 points. The decomposition depends on how one removes the mechanisms in a nonlinear model, but reversing their order in the appendix leaves their relative importance broadly intact. Weighting a household’s grocery basket therefore captures just one part of its financial exposure.

The consumption-tax experiment reduces energy and food taxes temporarily and assumes full pass-through to purchasers. Energy inflation in the 2022 simulation falls by 9.85 percentage points relative to the unchanged-tax case, and food inflation in 2023 falls by 1.62 points. The impact on the overall price index is smaller. In Table 6 the aggregate welfare loss falls from 6.65% to 6.41%. Savers benefit from both cheaper essentials and greater preservation of the purchasing power of nominal claims. Their modelled loss falls from 12.24% to 11.39%. Conversely, borrowers lose part of the real debt relief that inflation would have delivered. Their losses increase from 2.37% to 2.60%. A lower food or electricity bill can therefore coexist with a deterioration in a borrower’s lifetime position.

The authors match the cost of transfers to the cost of the tax cuts in each period. Matching just the discounted sum would allow one policy to pay households earlier, confounding timing with targeting. The resulting aggregate loss is 6.17%, a 0.48 percentage point improvement on the benchmark. For the bottom income quarter the loss falls from 6.51% to 5.42%. Borrowers retain the real erosion of outstanding liabilities and receive additional resources where eligible, taking their loss down to 2.00%. Households aged 65 and over do better under VAT relief. Their loss is 16.75% with the tax cuts and 17.06% with transfers, down from 18.20% without either. Figure 5 and Table 7 also show a modest cost in labour supply. Transfers reduce work somewhat more than VAT relief, especially among women deciding whether to participate. From the household’s perspective, avoiding costly extra work is part of the value of insurance. From the perspective of an output forecast, the change in participation would enter differently.

Appendix C asks how far the central result depends on real wages staying depressed. When real wages recover to their pre-crisis level by 2028, the no-policy loss falls to 6.05%, compared with 5.81% under the VAT cuts and 5.57% under transfers. The level of hardship changes materially, while the gap between instruments is almost unchanged in this scenario. For a monetary researcher, the distinction matters when an indirect tax change affects headline inflation. The observed price index may temporarily look better under VAT relief even if another use of the same budget would better protect disposable income. An estimate of the policy’s effect on inflation expectations, domestic demand or bond yields would require further evidence beyond this household model.

questions.question: Which households actually receive more insurance once benefit take-up and timing are observed?
questions.detail: Start with the bottom income quarter, where Table 6 reports a 1.09 percentage point welfare improvement with transfers. Link benefit eligibility, receipt and payment dates to disposable income, liquid savings and arrears. Spain’s Survey of Household Finances can supply asset and debt benchmarks. Administrative payment records would help distinguish late payment from non-take-up. Compare households around eligibility thresholds and report which households the bank or administrative sample misses.

questions.question: How much of an indirect tax cut reaches the household’s bill?
questions.detail: Use shop-level transaction prices and tariff schedules around each food and energy tax change to test the assumed full pass-through. Compare taxed products with closely matched untreated products. Separate wholesale energy moves, contract resets and retailer margins from a change in the tax. Reweight the resulting price changes using Spain’s Household Budget Survey and compare the protection for retirees with the paper’s Table 6 estimate.

questions.question: Does nominal debt position explain the difference between observed inflation and household hardship?
questions.detail: Combine household-specific price indices with nominal assets, debt repricing schedules, wages and the indexation of tax brackets and benefits. Check consumption and arrears among families with similar baskets but different net positions. The Survey of Household Finances and living-conditions survey could establish comparable groups before the shock. Follow them through the wage recovery to see whether one-year hardship and the model’s lifetime welfare ranking move together.
